title: Public Benefits Are a Hidden Engine of College Completion
gist: A RAND/Child Trends study of ~3,800 low-income young adults across 30 years of NLSY data finds EITC receipt raises next-year college enrollment odds 36% and SNAP receipt 63%, with each EITC year during enrollment tied to 40% higher graduation odds and a ~$18,400 annual bachelor's wage premium by the late 30s — arguing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's work-first rules misprice education as a competitor to employment rather than a complement.

insights.claim: Low-income young adults who received the Earned Income Tax Credit in a given year were 36 percent more likely to enroll in post-high-school education the following year than in years they did not receive it.
insights.speaker: Dana Thomson
insights.so_what: Refundable tax credits function as a de facto higher-education enrollment subsidy; changes to EITC parameters should be read as a leading indicator for community-college and regional-university enrollment.
insights.quote: Young adults who received the EITC in a given year were 36 percent more likely to enroll in post-high school education the following year than in years they did not receive it.

insights.claim: Receipt of SNAP food aid was associated with a 63 percent higher likelihood of enrolling in post-high-school education the following year — a larger effect than the EITC.
insights.speaker: Dana Thomson
insights.so_what: SNAP eligibility rules are an under-priced input to enrollment pipelines for community colleges and for-profit/regional education providers; tightening them is an enrollment headwind.
insights.quote: And they were 63 percent more likely to enroll if they received food aid through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP).

insights.claim: The binding constraint on college enrollment for low-income young adults is short-run cash flow — rent, food, basic expenses — not motivation or aspiration.
insights.speaker: Dana Thomson
insights.so_what: Interventions that relieve immediate liquidity (cash transfers, food aid) may move enrollment more per dollar than tuition-side subsidies.
insights.quote: It is often short-run financial constraints—not enough money to cover rent, food, or basic expenses while also paying for school—that keep young adults out of the classroom.

insights.claim: The findings rest on within-person year-over-year comparisons across nearly 30 years of Bureau of Labor Statistics National Longitudinal Survey of Youth data for a nationally representative sample of roughly 3,800 low-income adults aged 18 to 35, with controls for age, family income, and children.
insights.speaker: Dana Thomson
insights.so_what: The within-person design blunts the usual selection-bias objection, making this harder for opponents to dismiss and therefore more likely to shape legislative debate.
insights.quote: The trends we saw didn't stem from some subgroup with particularly high motivation; we were comparing the same person's behavior from one year to the next.
insights.locator: We used nearly 30 years of data

insights.claim: Each additional year a student received the EITC while enrolled was associated with 40 percent higher odds of graduating, meaning benefits affect persistence and not just initial enrollment.
insights.speaker: Dana Thomson
insights.so_what: Completion rates — not enrollment — drive the earnings premium and student-loan repayment performance, so benefit continuity during enrollment is a credit-quality variable.
insights.quote: each additional year students received the EITC while enrolled was associated with 40 percent higher odds of graduating
insights.locator: Once enrolled, benefits also help students stay.

insights.claim: Low-income adults in the study who earned a bachelor's degree were making about $18,400 more per year by their late 30s or early 40s than peers who worked but pursued no education beyond high school.
insights.speaker: Dana Thomson
insights.so_what: Quantifies the lifetime-income spread that public-benefit design is implicitly allocating; a concrete ROI number for arguments about education-linked benefit rules.
insights.quote: The low-income young adults in our study who got a bachelor's were making about $18,400 more a year by their late 30s or early 40s than peers who worked but did not pursue education beyond high school.

insights.claim: Graduate degree holders in the same low-income cohort earned roughly $40,600 more per year than working peers with no post-high-school education.
insights.speaker: Dana Thomson
insights.so_what: The convexity of the credential premium argues that marginal policy dollars aimed at persistence through advanced degrees carry outsized fiscal payback.
insights.quote: Graduate degree holders earned roughly $40,600 more.

insights.claim: Associate degree recipients showed no wage premium at all, yet had significantly lower poverty rates and were more likely to out-earn their parents — mobility without a measurable pay bump.
insights.speaker: Dana Thomson
insights.so_what: Undercuts wage-only ROI scorecards used to judge two-year programs; the value shows up in downside protection and mobility, not median salary.
insights.quote: Associate degree recipients didn't get the wage premium, but they showed significantly lower poverty rates and were more likely to earn more than their parents did

insights.claim: Financial aid only reaches students who have already enrolled, so public benefits and financial aid solve different problems: benefits clear the enrollment hurdle, aid sustains attendance afterward.
insights.speaker: Dana Thomson
insights.so_what: A clean mental model for evaluating access policy: subsidies gated on enrollment cannot fix an enrollment gap; look upstream for the marginal lever.
insights.quote: But financial aid only reaches people who already made it through the door.

insights.claim: Students enrolled at least half-time generally cannot receive SNAP, with exceptions only for work-study participants or those employed at least 20 hours per week — a rule that excludes many low-income students regardless of income.
insights.speaker: Dana Thomson
insights.so_what: A discrete, identifiable statutory rule that policymakers could change; watch for state waivers and reauthorization language as the actionable catalyst.
insights.quote: students enrolled at least half-time in higher education generally cannot receive SNAP
insights.locator: Yet too often benefit program rules work against that goal.

insights.claim: The 20-hour work exemption is self-defeating because research consistently finds academic progress deteriorates once students work that many hours.
insights.speaker: Dana Thomson
insights.so_what: The exemption designed to preserve benefits actively lowers completion odds, so the policy trades short-run labor supply for long-run earnings.
insights.quote: But research consistently finds that when students spend that many hours at a job, their academic progress begins to suffer.
insights.locator: Exceptions exist for those in a work-study program

insights.claim: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act's tightened work requirements embed a work-first framework that treats education and employment as competing priorities when the data show they are complementary routes to self-sufficiency.
insights.speaker: Dana Thomson
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific federal legislation whose implementation rules are the pressure point; enrollment declines at low-income-serving institutions would be the observable second-order effect.
insights.quote: Benefit program rules treat education and employment as competing priorities when they are, in fact, complementary paths to the same destination.
insights.locator: That's the core tension our findings highlight

insights.claim: An increasing share of jobs — including in health care, technology, and the skilled trades — require formal credentials, which raises the long-run cost of policies that push benefit recipients straight into work.
insights.speaker: Dana Thomson
insights.so_what: Credential inflation makes work-first rules progressively more costly over time; sectors facing licensed-labor shortages are the downstream casualty.
insights.quote: This is especially true as more and more jobs—including essential ones in health care, technology, and the skilled trades—require formal credentials.
insights.locator: That means benefit programs should be designed

insights.claim: States already have flexibility to count enrollment in workforce-linked college programs as meeting benefit work requirements, and several states have done so — no federal action required.
insights.speaker: Dana Thomson
insights.so_what: State-level adoption is the near-term, low-friction path; divergence across states creates a natural experiment and uneven enrollment trends by geography.
insights.quote: including the ability to count enrollment in workforce-linked college programs as meeting work requirements—something several states have already done
insights.locator: Practical steps are available right now.

insights.claim: Campus financial aid offices and public benefit systems operate as siloed systems, and coordinating them is a low-cost institutional fix for low-income student attrition.
insights.speaker: Dana Thomson
insights.so_what: Creates addressable demand for benefits-navigation and eligibility-screening services embedded in higher-ed student-services stacks.
insights.quote: And most campuses would benefit from coordinating the siloed financial aid and public benefit systems so that low-income students don't fall through the cracks.
insights.locator: Practical steps are available right now.
